title: Uncovering Nonstationary Dependence Among Drought Drivers: Identification and Modeling for Compound Drought Assessment
content:
Abstract

Hydrometeorological variables, such as precipitation, soil moisture, and streamflow are widely recognized to exhibit non-stationarity in their individual time series as human activities and climate change. In contrast, the extent to which the dependence structure linking these variables evolves over time remains poorly understood, despite its importance for characterizing compound droughts. Assuming stationary dependence may therefore obscure key drought dynamics and bias multivariate drought assessment. Hence, we proposes a diagnostic-driven framework that first investigate and model nonstationary dependence among drought drivers and subsequently develops a Non-stationary Integrated Drought Index (NIDI) for compound drought assessment. The framework combines a Bayesian dynamic model with Differential Evolution Markov Chain (DE-MC) inference and a time-sliding window approach to identify nonstationarity in both marginal drought behavior and intervariable dependence across meteorological, agricultural, and hydrological droughts. The approach is applied to the Krishna River Basin (India), a climatically heterogeneous and drought-prone region. Results provide clear evidence of time-varying dependence among precipitation, soil moisture, and streamflow, which is effectively captured by the proposed framework. Accounting for nonstationary dependence improves the identification of historical droughts, including major events in 1985, 1987, 2002–03, and 2012, and enhance detection of compound drought conditions relative to conventional stationary and univariate drought indices. The results demonstrate that evolving dependence plays a critical role in multivariate drought dynamics and that neglecting it can lead to underestimation of drought severity. The proposed framework provides a robust basis for monitoring compound droughts and offers insights for drought risk assessment under nonstationary hydroclimatic conditions.
